paras: The lynching of Craig and Parker Jordan was the hanging of two Black men by a mob in Leflore County, Mississippi, on the night of November 26, 1881, after they were accused of assassinating Robert Catlin, a white man. Both were said to have confessed after their capture and were hanged to a tree near a place the dispatches called Shepherdstown. Wire stories carried the case across the country, and Mississippi papers greeted it as "speedy vengeance."

Catlin lived on Bear Creek in Leflore County, across the Yazoo River from Holmes County. On a Thursday evening just after dark, as he sat by the fire with his wife and her brother, a young man named Barkham, a shot fired from outside the house struck him in the head and killed him. Writing before any arrest, the Lexington Bulletin said no one was suspected and no reason for the killing was known.

According to a Vicksburg Commercial dispatch from Yazoo City dated November 29, two Black men named Jordan and Craig were "hunted down and caught a day or two ago." They were said to have confessed, adding that they had lain in wait to shoot Mrs. Catlin as well and that they had also killed a peddler named Lowenstine, of which Catlin had gathered evidence. The Greenville Times wrote that the two were "arrested suspected of the crime" and hanged upon their confession.

They were "taken out and hanged to a tree" near Shepherdstown by what the dispatches called "the infuriated citizens." A special to the New York Herald from Greenwood, dated November 28, named them as Craig Jordan and Parker Jordan and placed the lynching on the night of November 26. The coverage does not say where the men were held, who made up the mob, or how many took part.

No report of an inquest or of any prosecution of the lynchers was found. On December 10 the Greenville Times reprinted further particulars from the Lexington Advertiser, which said Craig Jordan had stolen Catlin's skiff and that his uncle, Parker Jordan, urged the killing as revenge for two other Black men hanged years earlier for murdering Lowenstein. The Advertiser added that the plan had been known beforehand to "twenty or more negroes" who kept silent, and that Craig Jordan, "a popular preacher," preached to a large crowd the day after the killing.

All of the coverage came from white newspapers. The Herald's Greenwood special, which spelled the dead man's name "Calina," ran in the Washington Evening Star and the Richmond Dispatch on November 30. The New Orleans Times' Yazoo City special reached papers in Texas, Maine, New York and California by December 2, under headings such as "Hanged by Infuriated Citizens," with the name garbled as "Cattlin" or "Collins." The New-York Tribune ran it under "Four Negroes Lynched" beside a lynching at Oxford, North Carolina, and later digests said both happened "on the same night."

Papers in Mississippi and Memphis presented the hanging as deserved. The Memphis Public Ledger headed the Vicksburg dispatch "Judge Lynch. Swift but Deserved Vengeance," and the Greenville Times titled its notice "Speedy Vengeance." The Jackson Weekly Clarion called Craig Jordan "the colored assassin" and added "Shame!" that he was a preacher, while the Advertiser's "worst feature" of the case was the silence of Black residents. Every account rested the men's guilt on confessions attributed to them by their captors.

The Times and Commercial dispatches dated Catlin's killing to November 17, the Herald special to the 18th. Digests that put the lynching on "Thursday" or the night of the Oxford lynching conflict with the Greenwood special, which was dated November 28 and is the better evidence. The Louisiana Capitolian said three men were hanged; every other account gave two.

On motive, the Vicksburg Commercial and Greenville Times said the two had killed Lowenstein themselves and silenced Catlin as a witness, while the later Lexington Advertiser account said other men had been hanged for that murder.

reader.title: Lynching of Craig and Parker Jordan
bases: Two Black men accused of murdering a white man were hanged to a tree by 'infuriated citizens' or 'a mob' after their capture (A5, A4, A7).

Both men were hanged without trial by 'the infuriated citizens' or 'a mob' (A5, A7) after being captured and said to have confessed to assassinating a white man (A1, A24); the group's size is not given, but every account describes a body of citizens, not one or two men.

The Herald's Greenwood special (A1, A2) and the separate Times and Vicksburg Commercial dispatches from Yazoo City (A4, A5) independently report that two Black men accused of killing Catlin were lynched; only the number hanged (A7) and the dates differ.

framing.detail: Memphis Public Ledger headline 'JUDGE LYNCH. Swift but Deserved Vengeance Upon the Murderers of Robert Catlin.'
Greenville Times notice titled 'Speedy Vengeance', reporting the hanging upon confession without criticism.
Weekly Clarion calls Craig Jordan 'the colored assassin' and adds 'Shame!' that he was a preacher.
Lexington Advertiser (via Greenville Times) calls the 'worst feature' the silence of twenty or more Black residents who knew of the plan.
Herald Greenwood brief: 'LYNCHING IN MISSISSIPPI', a two-sentence item stating the confession as fact.
Times dispatch run under 'Hanged by Infuriated Citizens' (Sacramento) or 'Four Negroes Lynched' with the Oxford, N.C., case (New-York Tribune).
